notes: Independent Round-2 verifier answers. Only reviews/blind/H.json consulted. Special focus on kernel-level vs e2e speedup and per-scope version qualifications for quantization.

answers.rationale: A: FP16/BF16 halves memory footprint. C: FP32 accum mitigates catastrophic cancellation. D: downcast to FP16/BF16 introduces rounding error affecting training stability. B false — TC FP16 throughput exceeds FP32 GEMM on TC.
Swamping: once FP16 running sum > 2^k, values < ~2^(k-11) round to zero when added. Rewrite fixes it by keeping partial sums small and combining in FP32 at the end.

A: ~1% salient channels by activation magnitude. B: per-channel searched scale s; scaled salient weights round more accurately. C: W4A16, activations in FP16, scaling fused into preceding op. D false (AWQ ≠ GPTQ). E false (INT4 TC not required — dequant-in-register + FP16 TC works on Ampere+).

B: MinMax simplest; outliers inflate range. C: percentile discards top 0.1% for tighter range. D: KL-divergence entropy calibration (TensorRT default variant). A false — MinMax often worst on outlier-heavy activations.
Unpack two INT4 per byte → sign-extend to int8 → __int2half → multiply by per-group FP16 scale → feed FP16 TC. HBM traffic ~4× lower than FP16 storage while compute stays on FP16 TC.
FP32=(1,8,23); FP16=(1,5,10); BF16=(1,8,7). BF16 shares FP32's 8-bit exponent, sacrifices mantissa.
BF16's 8-bit exponent gives FP32-like dynamic range → mostly removes underflow/overflow risk; 7-bit mantissa is coarser than FP16's 10; loss scaling can often be simplified or removed.
TF32 = 19-bit internal TC input format: 1 sign, 8 exp (FP32 range), 10 mant (FP16 precision). Storage stays FP32; only TC multiplier truncates mantissa on input; accumulation is FP32.
Dynamic = compute activation scale from tensor stats at each forward. Static = calibrate offline; scales frozen as constants at runtime.
Forward correct (round→clamp→dequant). Because d/dx round = 0 almost everywhere, backward requires STE: d(round(x))/dx ≈ 1 within clamp region so gradients pass through as if identity.

A: E4M3 narrower range, higher mantissa — forward activations/weights. B: E5M2 wider range, lower precision — gradients. C: both 8 bits, choice is precision-vs-range. D false (scaling required). E false (FP8 TC debuted on Hopper/Ada, not Ampere).
A: Hopper FP8 TC ~2× BF16 throughput (compute-bound). C: FP32 accumulator regardless of input format. D: TE DelayedScaling maintains per-tensor scales. B false — accumulator is FP32, not FP8.

At M=1 batch-1 decode, kernel is bandwidth-bound: dominant cost is loading K×N weights (identical whether INT8 or FP16 activations, since weights dtype is unchanged); INT8 TC peak-TOPS can't be realized without compute per byte.
GPTQ: quantize column-by-column; after each column update remaining unquantized columns using per-layer Hessian (H ≈ 2 X^T X from calibration activations) to compensate for the just-introduced error.

A: per-tensor 1 scale, simplest. B: per-channel (per-row) applied in epilogue, cheap. C: per-group along in_channels, standard for W4A16 (group_size=128). D false (per-tensor accuracy < per-channel on non-uniform distributions). E false — per-group along K is legal, applied in inner loop per group.

PyTorch/NumPy broadcasting aligns the LAST axis; scale of shape (out,) would broadcast across the last axis of W (in_features), giving per-input-channel behavior. Fix: scale.unsqueeze(1) so it becomes (out, 1) and broadcasts across in_features.
Symmetric convention restricts range to be symmetric around zero: INT8 = [-127, 127], INT4 = [-7, 7]. This yields z=0 and simplifies GEMM.

A: INT4 KV kernel support less mature; often dequant-in-register to FP16. C: ~4× vs FP16, ~2× vs INT8 memory reduction. D: long-context QA more sensitive to INT4 KV due to softmax cumulative sensitivity. B false — INT4 is coarser than INT8 and generally less accurate for same calibration.

A: INT8 TC on Turing+ broadly. B: FP8 TC only on Hopper/Ada. C: W4A16 works on any FP16/BF16 TC via dequant-in-register — no INT4 TC required. D false (INT4 not deprecated on Hopper; W4A16 kernels use FP16 TC anyway). E false — CUDA-core software emulation of TC dtypes generally doesn't beat FP16 TC.
KV cache quantization reduces per-request KV memory footprint (allowing longer contexts / larger batches) and, if the attention kernel reads quantized KVs, reduces attention memory bandwidth.

KV quantization error accumulates through softmax as context grows: at 4K negligible, at 32K softmax's sensitivity to small logit changes over many attended positions surfaces the loss. Trade-off favorable if accuracy drop acceptable and batch-capacity gain valuable.

A: quantized-native attention kernel saves storage AND bandwidth. B: eager dequant to FP16 kills bandwidth savings. D: dequant-in-register still net-positive because HBM traffic drops. C false — mixed precision (FP16 weights + INT8 KV) is standard.

FP16 weights = 14 GB, W4A16 = ~3.5 GB + 0.11 GB scales ≈ 3.6 GB — factor ~4× reduction. Batch-1 decode is dominated by weight loading, so throughput improves close to that factor minus dequant overhead.

A: dynamic loss scaling for FP16. B: BF16's FP32-range removes need for loss scaling. C: FP16 in / FP32 accum / FP16 out matmul on TC. D: FP32 master weights preserve small-magnitude gradients that would round to zero in FP16.

Per-tensor MinMax dominated by ~1% outliers at ±50 → scale=0.394 → only ~5/254 levels for bulk of activations in [-2,2]. Per-channel activation quant or SmoothQuant (migrate outlier magnitude to weights) fixes it.
FP16 max ≈ 6.5e4; K=4096 accumulation of moderate partials easily exceeds → INF. FP32 (~3.4e38) safely accumulates; downcast-on-write to FP16 preserves output precision.

PTQ: quantize pretrained FP model with calibration set, no retraining. QAT: insert fake-quant ops during training so model learns quantization-robust weights — typically higher accuracy at low bit widths.

STE approximates d(round)/dx as identity within clamp region so gradients flow through fake-quant as no-op. Works well for INT8; becomes noisier at very low bit widths (INT2/INT3), motivating PACT/LSQ that learn better step sizes.

RNE: nearest with ties → even neighbor (IEEE 754 default; deterministic). Stochastic: probabilistic round in proportion to distance to each neighbor → unbiased estimator useful for very-low-precision training (BF16 / FP8 gradient accum).

Saturation clamps (200→127): loses extreme info but preserves ordinal relationships — mathematically desired for NNs. Wrap-around modular (200→-56): flips sign, catastrophic for signal-carrying activations.
Standard affine quantizer: q = round(x/s) + z; dequantize: x_hat = (q - z) * s. This is the ONNX / PyTorch / TensorRT convention.

SmoothQuant rewrites Y = XW = (X · diag(1/s)) · (diag(s) · W): activation channels smoothed (outlier magnitude reduced); weights absorb migrated magnitude. Since weights per-channel-quantize easily but activations usually per-tensor, this makes W8A8 tractable.
Symmetric z=0 → dequant = q*s; no zero-point cross-term in GEMM. Asymmetric uses full [0,255] and captures skewed distributions (post-ReLU) better, at cost of extra bias term.

Finer group size → more scale factors per weight matrix → each scale tracks narrower distribution → better accuracy but higher metadata bandwidth. Group=128 widely used default (~3% metadata overhead, most of accuracy captured).

C: W4A16 primarily targets bandwidth-bound decode; INT4 halves weight HBM traffic vs INT8; dequant-in-register keeps compute on FP16 TC. D: W8A8 uses INT8 TC for compute-bound scenarios; activations need dynamic or calibrated static scale. A false — dequant-in-register + FP16 TC works without INT4 TC. B false — W8A16 uses FP16 TC (not INT8) and doesn't need activation calibration since activations stay FP16.
